article.overview: A short-period seismometer is a seismometer built to be most sensitive to relatively rapid ground vibrations: roughly those that repeat about once per second or faster (frequencies of about 1 hertz up to a few tens of hertz). On the Moon such sensors record small, nearby and high-frequency events that long-period instruments miss or blur, including thermal moonquakes caused by the day–night temperature cycle, small meteoroid impacts, shallow moonquakes and the long, 'ringing' scattered signals typical of lunar seismograms. Every Apollo seismic station from Apollo 11 to Apollo 16 included one vertical short-period sensor (called SPZ) with a resonant period of 1 second [1][2]. Modern short-period sensors use micromachined silicon (MEMS) technology. India's ILSA operated on the Chandrayaan-3 lander in 2023 [22][23]. Others have been built but, as of this article's research date (12 November 2026), have not yet reached the Moon: the Short Period sensor of NASA's Farside Seismic Suite [13][20], the MEMS seismometer of China's Chang'e-7 lunar seismograph [28][29] and the short-period seismometer in NASA's Lunar Environment Monitoring Station [31][33].
article.description:
A seismometer measures how the ground moves. 'Short-period' describes the part of the vibration spectrum that the instrument is tuned to record. Seismic waves cover a very wide range of frequencies. Slow motions, with periods of tens to thousands of seconds, carry information about large-scale structure and tides. Faster vibrations, with periods of about one second or less, are produced by small and nearby sources and are strongly affected by fine-scale rock structure close to the surface. A short-period seismometer gives up sensitivity to the slowest motions in exchange for a compact, robust design that captures the faster ones well. There is no single formal boundary that defines 'short-period'. Each instrument is defined by its own published frequency response.

Two broad technologies have been used on the Moon or for lunar missions. The Apollo SPZ was a classical electromagnetic sensor: a magnet hanging on a spring moved relative to a coil and generated a voltage proportional to velocity [7][9]. Modern sensors are etched from single-crystal silicon. They include the InSight SP design used on Mars, its lunar derivative on the Farside Seismic Suite, India's ILSA and the MEMS channel of the Chang'e-7 seismograph [21][14][23][28]. Apollo flew a single vertical short-period component alongside three long-period components [1][2]. Modern lunar short-period sensors are generally three-component (triaxial), which lets scientists reconstruct the direction of ground motion [16][24][30].

A short-period seismometer is usually not deployed alone. It is generally paired with a long-period, broadband or very-broadband sensor in the same package, for example on Apollo, the Farside Seismic Suite, Chang'e-7 and LEMS. Together the pair covers a wide frequency band [2][16][28][30].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
Short-period seismometers serve several connected scientific goals on the Moon:

- **Thermal moonquakes and local activity.** The Apollo short-period sensors recorded many thousands of small, local events triggered by day–night temperature changes. Most of these thermal moonquakes can be seen only on the short-period instruments [7].
- **Shallow moonquakes.** The largest natural lunar events were first called 'high-frequency teleseismic' (HFT) events because their energy is concentrated above 1 Hz and shows clearly on short-period records [5][7]. Their amplitudes are consistent with sources in the upper mantle [6].
- **Meteoroid impacts and impact flux.** Many small impacts produce energy above the roughly 2 Hz upper limit of the Apollo long-period sensors and were detected mainly on the SPZ [2]. Counting these smaller impacts helps estimate how often meteoroids strike the Moon [5][6].
- **Scattering and near-surface structure.** Lunar seismic signals ring for a long time because the fractured, dry outer layers scatter seismic waves very strongly. Short-period data, analysed at several frequencies, constrain how heterogeneous the outer shell is and how weakly it absorbs seismic energy [3][5][8].
- **Operational and environmental monitoring.** High-frequency sensors also record lander, rover and astronaut activity. Apollo 14 short-period data captured the Lunar Module liftoff and many events attributed to venting and thermal 'popping' in the descent stage [3]. On Chandrayaan-3, ISRO attributed many ILSA signals to rover and instrument activity [22][25].
article.operating_principle:
Most seismometers rely on inertia. A proof mass is suspended inside a frame by a spring. When the ground moves, the frame moves with it, but the mass tends to lag behind. The instrument measures the relative motion between the mass and the frame.

Every mass-and-spring system has a natural (resonant) frequency at which it oscillates most easily. For ground vibrations faster than this frequency, the mass stays nearly still while the frame moves, so the relative motion closely follows the ground displacement. For slower vibrations the mass moves along with the frame and sensitivity falls. A short-period seismometer has a relatively high natural frequency, about 1 Hz (a period of 1 second) for the Apollo SPZ [1][7]. Damping stops the mass from ringing at its own resonance; Apollo's SPZ used a damping factor of 0.85 [7].

**Electromagnetic (Apollo).** In the Apollo SPZ a magnet served as the moving mass. It was suspended from the frame by a LaCoste spring and a triangular arrangement of 'delta rods', and as it moved it induced a voltage in a coil fixed to the frame. That voltage is proportional to the relative velocity between frame and mass [9]. The signal was amplified, high-pass and low-pass filtered (the low-pass anti-aliasing filter removes frequencies too high for the sample rate to capture faithfully), and digitised [7].

**Micromachined silicon (MEMS).** In the InSight SP design, the suspension and proof mass are etched from a single silicon wafer, and the proof mass has a fundamental vibration mode of 6 Hz. The sensor runs in feedback mode: coils plated onto the proof mass push it back towards its rest position, and the force needed to do this becomes the measurement [21]. ILSA's sensing elements are likewise made by bulk micromachining of silicon wafers [23]. ILSA uses separate 'fine-range' sensors for very small signals and 'coarse-range' sensors for strong motion [23][24].

**Digitisation and timing.** The analogue signal is converted to numbers at a fixed sampling rate. The rate must be at least twice the highest frequency of interest, which is why short-period channels are sampled much faster than long-period ones. The Apollo SPZ was recorded at a nominal 53 samples per second with 10-bit words, compared with about 5 samples per second for the long-period channels [10][7]. InSight's SP channels were digitised at 24 bits at 100 or 20 samples per second [21], and ILSA at 200 samples per second [23]. An accurate time stamp is essential so that signals at separate stations can be compared [7].
article.scientific_importance:
The Moon is seismically quiet compared with Earth, and its small events are dominated by high frequencies. Short-period sensors are therefore essential for building a complete picture of lunar seismicity. Most of the many thousands of events recorded on the Apollo short-period seismometers were small local moonquakes triggered by temperature changes, and most thermal moonquakes are visible only on the short-period instruments [7].

Short-period data were central to identifying shallow moonquakes, the most energetic natural moonquakes recorded. Their energy continues up to about 8 Hz before rolling off, which is why they were first called high-frequency teleseismic events [7]. Spectra of shallow moonquakes between 3 and 8 Hz show that the lunar interior absorbs very little seismic energy: the P-wave quality factor Q should be greater than 4000 at 3 Hz and between 4000 and 8000 at 8 Hz [8]. Multi-frequency analysis of artificial impacts, using short-period records at 2, 4 and 8 Hz, showed that the outer shell of the Moon may be heterogeneous on scales of 0.1 to 10 km to depths approaching 50–100 km [3].

Short-period data remain scientifically valuable today. Historically, the many events seen only on the short-period records were not catalogued [6], and most short-period data remained unanalysed because of numerous unnatural signals and noise spikes [11]. A recent re-analysis that denoised all the Apollo short-period data reported about 22,000 newly detected seismic events [11]. The resulting study added 46 shallow moonquakes to the 28 previously known [12].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a short-period seismometer. Each example below describes a specific instrument and states whether it has flown, is built but not yet flown, is heritage hardware from another planet, or is a design requirement. Where a value applies to a whole instrument package rather than to the short-period sensor alone, this is stated. Values that are not publicly specified are recorded as null. The examples use different technologies and are described in different units (velocity sensitivity, acceleration noise density, displacement detection), so their numbers should not be compared directly.

examples.name: Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment short-period vertical seismometer (SPZ)
examples.type: Historical lunar instrument (flown and operated on the Moon, 1969–1977)
examples.status: Flown: Apollo 11 (PSEP) and Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16 (ALSEP PSE)
examples.sensor_configuration: Single-axis, vertical short-period seismometer, one of four seismometers in each PSE (three long-period components plus one short-period vertical component).
examples.transducer: Coil-magnet velocity transducer with a moving magnet mass suspended by a LaCoste spring and delta rods.
examples.detection_threshold: Able to detect ground motions of 0.3 nm at 1 Hz (Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report).
examples.package_mass_note: Whole PSE including electronics module and thermal insulation (all four seismometers); not the SP sensor alone.

station_performance.Apollo 11: All four seismometers operated properly until the final 2 days, when the long-period sensors drifted; 21 days of operation (21 July–27 August 1969).
station_performance.Apollo 12: SPZ operated at reduced gain from activation; sources variously describe reduced sensitivity or failure to operate.
station_performance.Apollo 15: No SPZ-specific problem found in the sources reviewed.
station_performance.Apollo 16: High lunar-day temperatures from degraded thermal control (ALSEP Termination Report); NSSDCA attributes periodic excessive short-period noise to these temperatures.

examples.description:
The Apollo SPZ was a single-axis, vertical short-period seismometer with a resonant period of 1 second, mounted in the same Passive Seismic Experiment as three long-period sensors [1][2]. It was a coil-magnet velocity transducer [7][9]. Its response parameters included a damping factor of 0.85, a generator constant of 175 V/(m/s) and a pre-amplifier gain of 23,700 [7]. The SP seismometer covered 0.05 to 20 Hz [2], and its displacement response peaked at about 8 Hz [7]. It could detect ground motions of 0.3 nm at 1 Hz [2]. At the ALSEP stations SPZ data were sampled at a nominal 53 samples per second, and the actual rate varied slightly [10], with 10-bit digitisation (0–1023 digital units) [7][3].

The 11.5 kg mass, 23 cm × 29 cm sensor unit and 4.3–7.4 W power range belong to the whole PSE, not the SP sensor alone [2]. No SP-only mass is published. The Apollo 11 system as a whole (the PSEP, including its solar power) weighed 48 kg [1].

Station performance differed. At Apollo 11 all four seismometers worked until the final two days of the 21-day mission [1]. The Apollo 12 SPZ operated at reduced gain from activation [2][4][5]. At Apollo 14 the SPZ operated as planned [3]. The Apollo 16 experiment ran hot during the lunar day because of degraded thermal control [4], and NSSDCA attributes periodic excessive noise in its short-period seismometer to those high temperatures [36].

examples.name: Farside Seismic Suite (FSS) Short Period (SP) sensor
examples.type: Modern lunar flight hardware (built and tested; not yet flown)
examples.status: Flight hardware built and tested (passed thermal-vacuum testing June 2024); CLPS task order CP-12 ended July 2026; no replacement lander identified in the sources reviewed.
examples.builder: Kinemetrics, Inc., with design work at Imperial College London and the University of Oxford.
examples.sensor_configuration: Three-component (triaxial) micromachined silicon sensor; new build based on the InSight SP design; complements the vertical Very Broadband (VBB) seismometer.
examples.form: Gold, puck-shaped device holding sensors etched into three square silicon chips, each about 1 inch (25 mm) wide.
examples.suite_design_operating_duration: At least 4½ months (FSS suite; mission design, not a sensor lifetime).
examples.description:
The FSS Short Period sensor was built by Kinemetrics in collaboration with the University of Oxford and Imperial College London, based on a design used on InSight [13][15]. It is a compact micromachined silicon design providing three-component sensitivity to complement the ultra-sensitive vertical Very Broadband seismometer [16]. NASA describes it as a gold, puck-shaped device that measures motion in three directions using sensors etched into three square silicon chips about 1 inch (25 mm) wide [14]. A 2025 abstract calls it 'the most sensitive and mature compact triaxial sensor available for space application' [18].

The suite as a whole is self-sufficient, with independent power, communications and thermal control for surviving the lunar night [17], and is designed to operate for at least 4½ months [13]. The hardware passed thermal-vacuum testing in June 2024 [18] and was then placed in storage to await its lander [19]. Its planned CLPS delivery (task order CP-12) was ended in July 2026 [20]. No FSS-specific frequency band, noise floor, mass or power for the SP sensor was found in public sources.

examples.name: InSight SEIS Short Period (SP) sensors (Mars heritage)
examples.type: Flown heritage hardware on Mars (not a lunar instrument)
examples.status: Flown and operated on Mars (NASA InSight); included only as design heritage for the FSS SP sensor.
examples.builder: Sensors designed by Imperial College London; electronics developed by the University of Oxford and Kinemetrics.
examples.sensor_configuration: Three SP axes: SP1 vertical; SP2 and SP3 horizontal, separated by 60° in azimuth.
examples.transducer: Single-crystal silicon suspension and proof mass made by through-wafer deep reactive-ion etching (fundamental mode 6 Hz), operated in feedback mode with electromagnetic actuation from coils plated on the proof mass.
examples.self_noise_requirement: Better than 1e-8 m/s²/√Hz between 0.1 and 1 Hz (requirement).
examples.self_noise_measured: 3e-9 m/s²/√Hz at 2.5 s period, measured in a low-noise seismic vault on Earth.
examples.mass_note: Three SP sensors in their boxes with their feedback card, excluding tethers.
examples.power_note: Only the whole-SEIS figure (about 5.9 W in normal operating mode) is published.
examples.description: InSight's SEIS experiment carried two sets of three-axis seismometers, very-broadband and short-period. Its SP sensors were designed by Imperial College, and the electronics were developed by Oxford University and Kinemetrics [21]. Each SP sensor's suspension and proof mass are micromachined from single-crystal silicon, with a fundamental vibrational mode of 6 Hz, and operate in feedback mode with electromagnetic actuation [21]. The SPs target a 0.1–50 Hz bandwidth [21]. They were required to achieve self-noise better than 10⁻⁸ m/s²/√Hz between 0.1 and 1 Hz, and measured 3 × 10⁻⁹ m/s²/√Hz at a 2.5 s period in a low-noise vault on Earth [21]. The three sensors with their boxes and feedback card had a mass of 614 g [21]. They were digitised at 24 bits [21] and designed to operate at up to 15° tilt [21]. These are Mars-mission values shown as heritage only; they are not measured lunar performance.

examples.name: ILSA — Instrument for Lunar Seismic Activity (Chandrayaan-3 Vikram lander)
examples.type: Flown lunar instrument (operated on the Moon, 24 August–3 September 2023)
examples.status: Flown and operated on the Moon (ISRO Chandrayaan-3, 2023). Developed at LEOS, Bangalore.
examples.classification_note: ISRO's PRADAN archive calls ILSA a 'short period type seismometer'; the 2020 design paper describes it as a 'broadband strong motion' sensor.
examples.sensor_configuration: Cluster of six MEMS accelerometers: three fine-range and three coarse-range sensors (three-axis).
examples.description:
ILSA was a three-axis MEMS instrument designed and built at LEOS, Bangalore. ISRO described it as the first instrument based on MEMS technology on the Moon [22]. Its cluster of six high-sensitivity accelerometers recorded ground acceleration continuously from 24 August to 3 September 2023, at 200 samples per second, using three fine-range and three coarse-range sensors [23]. ISRO's data archive calls it a 'short period type seismometer' [23]. The 2020 design paper, written for the Chandrayaan-2 lander unit, classifies it as a broadband strong-motion sensor. It gives a resolution of 100 nano-g/√Hz up to ±0.5 g over a 40 Hz bandwidth, a mass of 1.8 kg, a size of 170 × 170 × 72 mm and power below 4 W [24]. The fine-range sensors operate up to 1.5 milli-g and the coarse-range sensors up to 0.5 g [24]. The qualification model achieved about 100 nano-g/√Hz in ground tests [24]. Whether these Chandrayaan-2 design values apply unchanged to the Chandrayaan-3 flight unit has not been confirmed.

ISRO reported an apparently natural event on 26 August 2023 [22]. The first results paper characterised the recorded signals and attributed many of them to rover and instrument activity [25]. An independent re-analysis found no positive evidence that the candidate natural events were natural [26].

examples.name: Chang'e-7 lunar seismograph — MEMS seismometer channel
examples.type: Lunar flight hardware (not yet launched); values are design requirements
examples.status: Assigned to the Chang'e-7 lander; launch did not proceed in its planned 2026 window; no new date found as of 12 November 2026.
examples.sensor_configuration: Lunar seismograph containing a broadband seismometer and a MEMS seismometer; the MEMS channel covers the short-period band.
examples.description: The Chang'e-7 lander's four scientific payloads include a lunar seismograph covering 1/120–100 Hz with a dynamic range greater than 120 dB [27]. A 2026 calibration paper lists the mission-required specifications for its two sensors [28]. The MEMS seismometer channel is specified for 1–100 Hz, self-noise better than 16 × 10⁻⁹ g/√Hz at 10 Hz, a range of 16 × 10⁻⁹ to 16 × 10⁻³ g, a sensitivity of 187 ± 20 V/g and a dynamic range greater than 120 dB. The companion broadband seismometer is specified for 1/120–10 Hz [28]. The paper describes the instrument as China's first independently developed lunar seismograph, designed for an eight-year operational lifetime (a design target) [28]. All of these are requirements, not measured lunar performance, and the source does not use the term 'short-period'. Mass and power are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Xinhua reported on 23 August 2026 that the Chang'e-7 launch would not proceed in its planned window that year [29].

examples.name: Lunar Environment Monitoring Station (LEMS) short-period seismometer
examples.type: Lunar flight hardware (flight-accepted; not yet assigned to a mission)
examples.status: LEMS completed and accepted for flight in 2026; stored at NASA Goddard until assigned to an Artemis mission.
examples.builder: University of Maryland-led LEMS; seismometers from the University of Arizona Planetary Seismometer Lab with Silicon Audio.
examples.sensor_configuration: Three-axis short-period seismometer, paired with a three-axis broadband seismometer (per 2025 abstract; a 2026 news release describes 'two sets of identical sensors').
examples.self_noise: 2.0e-9 m/s²/√Hz at 10 Hz (unit printed as m/s²/Hz on the source page; probably /√Hz).
examples.lems_station_weight_note: NASA gives LEMS as weighing 11 pounds in lunar gravity (a lunar weight, not a mass).
examples.mission_concept: Astronaut-deployed with buried sensors; three-month threshold mission, two-year baseline operation.
examples.description: LEMS is designed as an astronaut-deployed seismic station. A 2025 abstract describes it as carrying a three-axis short-period seismometer and a complementary three-axis broadband seismometer, both buried by astronauts, for a three-month threshold mission and a two-year baseline [30]. The University of Arizona's lab, which partners with Silicon Audio, states that its SP sensor is most sensitive above 1 Hz, with a self-noise floor of 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ m/s²/√Hz at 10 Hz. It also states that a triaxial unit is about 1 kg and requires 250 mW, and that the sensor has been developed to TRL 8 for the lunar south-pole environment [31]. These are developer-stated values, and the source page prints the noise unit as m/s²/Hz. A 2026 university news release instead describes 'two sets of identical sensors' [32], a discrepancy that is unresolved. NASA completed LEMS in 2026 and is storing it at Goddard until it is assigned to an Artemis mission [33]. Artemis III has been re-planned as a 2027 test flight in low Earth orbit [34].

physical_specifications.other_concepts: Japan's LUNAR-A mission was to deliver two-axis lunar seismometers on penetrators, but it was cancelled in early 2007 [35]. Secondary sources describe its seismometer as short-period, but that was not confirmed from an official page. The Lunar Geophysical Network, a proposed multi-station geophysics mission, has been prioritised in the planetary science Decadal Survey as a candidate New Frontiers mission [18]. It is a concept, not built hardware.
physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No short-period-sensor-only dimensions are published for Apollo. The 23 cm diameter × 29 cm height figure is the whole Passive Seismic Experiment sensor unit containing four seismometers [2]. Modern MEMS short-period sensors are far smaller. The InSight and FSS SP devices are built around square silicon dies about 25 mm (1 inch) wide [14], and the Chandrayaan-2 ILSA design measures 170 × 170 × 72 mm [24]. Actual envelope dimensions for the FSS SP, Chang'e-7 MEMS seismometer and LEMS SP sensor are not publicly specified.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Published masses vary with what is included. The Apollo PSE weighed 11.5 kg including its electronics module and thermal insulation, which covers all four seismometers [2]. InSight's three SP sensors, in their boxes with their feedback card, had a mass of 614 g, excluding tethers [21]. The ILSA design is listed at 1.8 kg [24]. The University of Arizona states that a triaxial short-period sensor of the LEMS type is about 1 kg [31]. NASA gives LEMS as a whole as weighing 11 pounds in the Moon's low gravity, a lunar weight rather than a mass [33]. Masses for the FSS SP sensor and the Chang'e-7 MEMS seismometer are not publicly specified.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Apollo PSE total power varied between 4.3 and 7.4 W for the whole experiment [2]. The ILSA design draws less than 4 W [24]. The LEMS-type triaxial short-period sensor requires about 250 mW [31]. InSight's SEIS used about 5.9 W for the entire experiment in normal operating mode, with no SP-only figure published [21]. Power for the FSS SP sensor and the Chang'e-7 MEMS seismometer is not publicly specified. Survival heating during the roughly two-week lunar night, and the battery or radioisotope power behind it, usually dominates the energy budget rather than the sensor itself [1][17].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Short-period seismometers face several lunar environmental challenges, each with an operational consequence:

- **Temperature extremes and drift.** Surface temperatures swing strongly between lunar day and night. On Apollo, small changes in the actual sampling rate were observed at all sites, partly because of large temperature variations [7]. At Apollo 16, degraded thermal control led to high temperatures during the lunar day [4], which NSSDCA links to periodic excessive noise in the short-period seismometer [36]. Apollo 11's solar-powered package could operate only during the lunar day [1]. The Farside Seismic Suite was designed with independent power, communications and thermal control so that it can survive and operate through the lunar night [17].
- **Self-generated and lander noise.** Because short-period sensors are sensitive to high-frequency vibration, nearby hardware can swamp them. At Apollo 14 most short-period events were attributed to gas venting and thermoelastic 'popping' in the Lunar Module descent stage [3]. On Apollo 12, square-wave pulses on the SPZ trace were suspected to come from an analogue-to-digital converter malfunction [2].
- **Ground coupling and levelling.** The sensor must be firmly coupled to the regolith and close to level. InSight's SP sensors were designed to operate at up to a 15° tilt from vertical [21]. LEMS seismometers are planned to be buried by astronauts to improve coupling and thermal stability [30].
- **Dynamic range.** The instrument must record tiny natural signals without saturating when nearby activity is strong. ILSA handles this with separate fine-range sensors (up to 1.5 milli-g) and coarse-range sensors (up to 0.5 g) [24]. The Chang'e-7 seismograph requirements specify a dynamic range greater than 120 dB [28].
- **Timing and data handling.** Short-period channels produce more data than long-period channels because they are sampled faster. Time stamps must be reliable: errors of up to one minute between the Apollo software clock and real time were later identified [7]. Some Apollo short-period samples were displaced by other telemetry words and must be interpolated in modern archives [10].
article.limitations:
- A short-period seismometer is not designed for the slowest ground motions. Low-frequency signals such as tides and long-period surface waves require long-period, broadband or very-broadband sensors, which is why short-period sensors are usually paired with one.
- A single station cannot uniquely locate most events. Distances and depths need several stations or additional assumptions.
- Short-period records are easily contaminated by local noise from landers, rovers, heaters and thermal cracking. This makes it harder to tell natural from artificial events. An independent re-analysis of Chandrayaan-3 ILSA data found no positive evidence that its natural moonquake or impact candidates were natural [26].
- Hardware degradation is hard to correct after deployment. The Apollo 12 SPZ operated at reduced gain from activation, with its mass apparently rubbing slightly on the frame [2], and later reports describe it as having reduced sensitivity [4] or as having failed to operate since activation [5].
- High sampling rates mean large data volumes, which strain lander downlink, relay communications and storage.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A short-period seismometer is a surface payload. It can be delivered as part of a larger astronaut-deployed experiment package (Apollo, LEMS), as a self-contained robotic payload on a commercial lander (Farside Seismic Suite), or as an instrument mounted on a lander (ILSA on Chandrayaan-3, the seismograph planned for the Chang'e-7 lander). The sensor's sensitivity to vibration and temperature shapes every stage of transport and deployment.
transportation_process: Integrate and calibrate on Earth. The sensor is mounted in its housing, calibrated, and tested against launch vibration, thermal-vacuum and (for some designs) simulated lunar gravity. For example, the FSS hardware passed thermal-vacuum testing in June 2024 [18].

Lock or protect the proof mass for launch. Launch and landing loads are far larger than the signals the instrument is designed to detect, so the design must survive them without damaging the suspension. Specific caging methods are instrument-specific and are not described in the sources used here.
Launch and lunar transfer. The payload rides on a lander or crewed vehicle. It must stay within thermal limits during cruise and, for long-lived payloads, keep its battery healthy.
Landing and deployment. The payload is either operated in place on the lander or carried and placed on the surface. Placing it away from the lander reduces lander-generated noise.
Levelling, coupling and thermal protection. The sensor is levelled (or tolerates tilt), coupled to the ground, and thermally insulated. Burial is planned for LEMS [30].

Power, data and timing. The sensor is connected to its power source (solar, battery or radioisotope), data handling and a reliable time reference, then commissioned with calibration signals. Apollo sensors were calibrated by commanding current steps into each seismometer's coil from Earth [2].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo short-period sensors were deployed by astronauts as part of the Passive Seismic Experiment. At the ALSEP stations of Apollo 12 to 16 the experiment was connected to a central station powered by radioisotope thermoelectric generators, which allowed continuous operation [4]. Apollo 11's earlier, simpler package used solar cells and could operate only during the lunar day [1]. The Farside Seismic Suite is designed as a self-sufficient robotic payload with independent power, communications and thermal control, so that it can outlive its lander [17]. ILSA was mounted on the Vikram lander and operated from 24 August to 3 September 2023 [23]. LEMS is designed for astronaut deployment, with buried sensors, a three-month threshold mission and a two-year baseline [30].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo provides the only flown examples of astronaut-deployed short-period seismometers. They were placed on the Moon on 21 July 1969 (Apollo 11), 19 November 1969 (Apollo 12), 5 February 1971 (Apollo 14), 31 July 1971 (Apollo 15) and 21 April 1972 (Apollo 16), and the network was switched off on 30 September 1977 [1][4]. ILSA on Chandrayaan-3 (2023) is the flown example of a lander-mounted MEMS short-period-type instrument [22][23].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with any specific lander, rover or crewed vehicle is asserted here. The Farside Seismic Suite was built for delivery under NASA CLPS task order CP-12, but that task order was ended by mutual agreement in July 2026 [20]. No replacement lander had been identified in the sources reviewed. The Chang'e-7 launch did not proceed in its planned 2026 window [29]. LEMS was completed and is being stored until it is assigned to an Artemis mission [33], and NASA has re-planned Artemis III as a crewed test flight in low Earth orbit in 2027 [34]. Any future pairing would need verified interface data: mass, envelope, mounting, launch and landing loads, isolation from lander vibration, thermal environment, power (including lunar-night survival), data rate and time synchronisation.

article.historical_significance:
The Apollo 11 short-period sensor made the first high-frequency seismic recordings on another world. It recorded 'a great variety of high-frequency (2 to 18 Hz) signals' during its 21 days of operation in July and August 1969 [1]. The later Apollo SPZ sensors operated as part of the four-station network until it was shut down on 30 September 1977 [4][7]. Short-period data from that network revealed thermal moonquakes [7], helped identify shallow moonquakes [5][7], and improved estimates of meteoroid flux [5]. They also showed that the outer layers of the Moon scatter seismic waves extremely strongly and absorb little seismic energy [3][8].

Chandrayaan-3's ILSA, which ISRO described as the first instrument based on MEMS technology on the Moon, marked the first lunar seismic measurements since Apollo. It recorded an apparently natural event on 26 August 2023 whose source ISRO said was under investigation [22]; an independent re-analysis later questioned the natural origin of such candidates [26]. The Farside Seismic Suite, LEMS and the Chang'e-7 seismograph each carry a short-period sensor built for the Moon, but none had reached the Moon as of November 2026 [20][29][33].

article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- 'Short-period seismometer' names a class of instruments, not one design. The examples here differ in technology, axes, units of sensitivity and status, and their numbers are not interchangeable.
- No published frequency band, noise floor, mass or power was found for the Farside Seismic Suite SP sensor itself. The InSight values are Mars heritage, not measured FSS performance.
- ILSA specifications come from the 2020 design paper for the Chandrayaan-2 unit. That they apply unchanged to the Chandrayaan-3 flight unit is assumed, not confirmed. ISRO's data archive calls ILSA a 'short period type seismometer', while the design paper describes it as a broadband strong-motion sensor.
- Chang'e-7 values are mission-required specifications (design requirements), not measured performance. The source does not use the term 'short-period' for its MEMS channel; the classification here is inferred from its 1–100 Hz band.
- LEMS sources conflict. A 2025 abstract describes one short-period and one broadband three-axis seismometer [30], while a 2026 university news release refers to 'two sets of identical sensors' [32]. The University of Arizona lab page prints the SP noise unit as m/s²/Hz, which is probably intended to be m/s²/√Hz [31].
- Apollo 12 SPZ status is described differently across sources: reduced gain [2], reduced sensitivity at low signal levels [4], or failure to operate since activation [5]. No explicit SPZ status statement was found for Apollo 15; normal operation is inferred from the absence of reported problems.
- The figure of about 22,000 newly detected Apollo short-period events comes from a conference abstract [11]; the full peer-reviewed paper was not consulted.
- Mission status (FSS delivery, Chang'e-7 launch, LEMS assignment) reflects sources available on 12 November 2026 and may change.
- Lunar landing-site or location recommendations are deliberately not included; the user has deferred them.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url, source_page_url, source_urls and reference url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Where removal would make a URL unusable (NSSDCA), the URL is null and the identifier is given. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Direct image URLs were checked for HTTP 200 and an image content type on 2026-11-12.

data_quality_notes: catalogue_id is set to the catalogue payload ID (3). The v4 reference (payload 001) uses catalogue_id 1, so its meaning is ambiguous; the Explorer app does not read this field.
Payload name uses the exact catalogue spelling 'Short-period seismometer'. The v4 reference capitalised its name ('Passive Seismometer'), which differs from the catalogue.

Reference 36 (NSSDCA Apollo 16 PSE record) has url null in JSON because NSSDCA pages require the query parameter id=1972-031C-01; removing the query string makes the URL unusable. The Markdown gives the full link. Other NSSDCA pages were not used for the same reason.
No FSS-specific SP sensor band, noise, mass or power were found; InSight SP values are Mars heritage only.

ILSA specifications are from the Chandrayaan-2 design paper; their equivalence to the Chandrayaan-3 flight unit is assumed, not confirmed. ISRO classifies ILSA inconsistently ('short period type' versus 'broadband strong motion').
Chang'e-7 MEMS values are design requirements (task-required specifications), not measurements; 'short-period' classification is inferred from the 1–100 Hz band.
LEMS: conflicting descriptions (SP + broadband versus 'two sets of identical sensors'); noise unit printed as m/s²/Hz on the developer page; mission assignment pending.
Apollo 12 SPZ status differs across sources (reduced gain, reduced sensitivity, failed). Apollo 15 SPZ normal operation is inferred from the absence of reported problems.

The ~22,000 newly detected Apollo short-period events is from a conference abstract; the peer-reviewed Onodera (2024) JGR Planets paper was not read in full. Duennebier & Sutton (1974), Nakamura (1977) and Gillet et al. (2017) are cited only through reviews.
Quotes from web pages (NSSDCA, JAXA DARTS, EGU, Eos and several news pages) were obtained through a web-fetch summary rather than a raw page read; PDF sources were read as extracted text.

Image rights: PIA22926 is credited to Imperial College London; the Chang'e-7 diagram is a journal figure with unverified licence; ISRO website reuse terms not verified. The ILSA plot and PIA22926 JPEG are low resolution.
No official public image asset of an actual Apollo SPZ seismogram was found; the S69-59547 seismogram is very probably not an SPZ record and is captioned accordingly.
The proof-mass launch-locking step in transportation_process is a generic engineering consideration; no instrument-specific caging mechanism was sourced.
Mission status statements reflect sources available on 2026-11-12.
